tool.name: NLTK
tool.tagline: The Natural Language Toolkit: classic NLP algorithms, corpora and teaching tools
tool.description: NLTK is a Python library of classic natural language processing building blocks: tokenizers, stemmers, taggers, parsers, WordNet, sentiment lexicons and many text corpora. It is widely used for teaching, research prototypes and lightweight text preprocessing. Learning it gives you a clear, hands-on understanding of how NLP pipelines work under the hood.

glossary.def: Getting computers to work with human language: splitting text into words, finding names, judging tone, translating and so on.
An extra download NLTK keeps separate from the library itself, such as a word list, a collection of texts or a small pretrained model. You fetch it with nltk.download().
One piece of text after it has been split up: usually a word, a number or a punctuation mark.
NLTK's sentence splitter: a model that learned from lots of text which periods end a sentence and which belong to abbreviations like 'Dr.'.
A large collection of English news sentences that people labelled by hand with their grammar. Its rules for splitting words and its list of word tags became a standard that NLTK follows.
A count of how often each item, usually each word, occurs in a text. NLTK's FreqDist holds one.
A very common word such as 'the', 'of' or 'and' that says little about what a text is about, and is often removed before counting.
A collection of texts gathered for study, such as a set of books, news articles or reviews.
An NLTK object that loads a corpus and offers the same methods, like words() and sents(), for every collection.
A list-like object returned by a corpus reader. It reads text from disk only when you use it, so a huge corpus doesn't fill your computer's memory.
Cutting words down to a shared base by chopping off endings with fixed rules, so 'connected' and 'connecting' both become 'connect'. The result need not be a real word.
The dictionary form of a word, the one you would look up: 'run' for 'ran', 'mouse' for 'mice'.
Turning each word into its dictionary form (its lemma) using a word list and rules: 'ran' becomes 'run', 'mice' becomes 'mouse'.
A large English dictionary built for programs. It groups words by meaning and records how meanings relate, such as 'a dog is a kind of animal'.
A short label saying what kind of word a token is in its sentence: noun, verb, adjective and so on. NLTK writes them as codes like NN (noun) and VB (verb).
The full list of labels a part-of-speech tagger can give. NLTK uses the detailed Penn Treebank list by default, or a simpler 'universal' one.
A run of n tokens in a row. A bigram is two ('New York'), a trigram three ('New York City').
Words that appear together more often than chance would predict, such as 'strong tea' or 'New York'.
A formula that scores how strongly two words belong together. It is used to rank possible collocations.
An association measure that compares how often two words appear together with how often you would expect if they were unrelated. It overrates very rare pairs.
Judging whether a piece of text sounds positive, negative or neutral, for example whether a review liked the product.
A rule-based sentiment analysis tool in NLTK, tuned for short social media posts. It scores words from a word list and adjusts for 'not', 'very', capital letters and '!'.
A word list with extra information about each word. VADER's lexicon gives each word a positive or negative score.
In NLTK, one example prepared for a classifier: a dict of clues about it (its features), such as {'has(great)': True}.
A function you write that turns a document into a featureset, the dict of clues a classifier learns from.
A simple classifier that, for each label, multiplies how likely each clue is under that label, then picks the label with the highest result. Fast and easy to inspect.
Grouping part-of-speech-tagged words into short phrases that don't overlap, such as noun phrases like 'the old cat'. Also called shallow parsing.
A nested structure showing how a sentence breaks into parts: the sentence contains phrases, phrases contain smaller phrases, down to single words.
Finding names in text and saying what kind they are: a person, an organisation, a place and so on.
A way to write chunks as one tag per token: B- marks the first token of a chunk, I- a token inside it, and O a token outside any chunk.
In WordNet, a set of words that share one meaning, such as car, auto and automobile. A word with several meanings belongs to several synsets.
A more general meaning: 'canine' is a hypernym of 'dog', because a dog is a kind of canine.
A more specific meaning: 'puppy' is a hyponym of 'dog', because a puppy is a kind of dog.
A part-whole link in WordNet: 'trunk' is a meronym (a part) of 'tree', and 'tree' is a holonym (the whole) of 'trunk'.
One particular meaning of a word: 'bank' has a river-edge sense and a money sense.
A set of rewrite rules that describe how sentences are built, such as 'a sentence is a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase'.
In a grammar, a label like S or NP that stands for a group of words and is rewritten by rules until only actual words remain.
A parser that stores every partial result in a table (the chart) and reuses it, so it finds all possible trees without redoing work.
A model that gives a probability to a sequence of words: how likely it is that someone would write it. N-gram models do this by counting; LLMs are huge modern ones.
Moving a little probability from things a model has seen to things it hasn't, so an unseen word sequence gets a small chance instead of zero.
A score of how surprised a language model is by test text, roughly how many words it is choosing between at each step. Lower is better.
Of the items a system labelled as X, the share that really are X. High precision means few false alarms.
Of the items that really are X, the share the system found. High recall means few misses.
One number that combines precision and recall; it stays low if either of them is low.
A grid that counts, for each true label, how often a system predicted each label, so you can see which labels it mixes up.
The fewest single-letter insertions, deletions or replacements that turn one word into another: 'kitten' to 'sitting' is 3.
A score of how much two people labelling the same items agree, after removing the agreement they would reach by pure chance. 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level.
A score for machine translation: how many short word sequences in the output also appear in human reference translations, with a penalty for output that is too short.

concepts.name: Installing NLTK and its data
concepts.summary: Install the NLTK library, download the extra data it needs (word lists, example texts, small models) and tell NLTK where to find it.
concepts.why: Most NLTK errors on a new computer are about missing data, not mistakes in your code.
concepts.body:
**Natural language processing** (NLP) means getting computers to work with human language: splitting text into words, counting them, judging whether a review is positive. **NLTK**, the Natural Language Toolkit, is a Python library full of ready-made NLP tools.

NLTK comes in two parts. The Python package itself is installed with `pip install nltk`. The second part is a separate collection of **data packages**: word lists, collections of example texts, and small **pretrained models**, which are files of patterns NLTK learned in advance from lots of example text. Many NLTK tools can't do anything until their data package is downloaded.

`nltk.download("name")` fetches one data package into a folder called `nltk_data`, usually in your home directory (your personal folder, like `/home/ana` or `C:\Users\ana`). Packages you'll meet early:

- `punkt_tab`: the model that splits text into sentences
- `stopwords` (lists of very common words) and `wordnet` (a big English word list with meanings)
- `averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng`, which labels words as nouns, verbs and so on
- `vader_lexicon` for judging positive or negative tone, and example texts such as `gutenberg`, `brown` and `movie_reviews`

If a package is missing, NLTK raises a `LookupError`, the exception it uses for "I couldn't find that data". Its message names the exact package to download, so read it: it tells you the fix.

`nltk.data.path` is a list of the folders NLTK searches, in order. To keep the data somewhere else, such as inside your project, set the `NLTK_DATA` **environment variable**: a named setting your computer hands to every program it starts, here holding a folder path. Or download straight into a folder with `nltk.download("stopwords", download_dir=path)`.

If your program will run on another computer, such as a server that answers many users, download the data once while setting that computer up, not every time the program runs. Then the program never waits on the internet or breaks without it. You can also download from the terminal: `python -m nltk.downloader stopwords punkt_tab`.
concepts.code:
import nltk

for pkg in ["punkt_tab", "stopwords", "wordnet"]:
    nltk.download(pkg, quiet=True)          # does nothing if already downloaded

print(nltk.__version__)                     # e.g. 3.9.2
print(nltk.data.path[0])                    # first folder NLTK searches

try:
    nltk.data.find("corpora/not_a_real_corpus")
except LookupError as e:
    print("LookupError:", "not_a_real_corpus" in str(e))   # True

print(nltk.data.find("corpora/stopwords") is not None)     # True: installed

# The same from a terminal:
#   python -m nltk.downloader punkt_tab stopwords wordnet
#   NLTK_DATA=/opt/nltk_data python app.py
takeaways: The pip package and the data packages are installed separately
`nltk.download(name)` fetches data; a LookupError message names what is missing
`NLTK_DATA` and `nltk.data.path` control where NLTK looks for data
On a server, download data once during setup, not while the program runs
pitfalls: Calling nltk.download every time a user does something in your app, so it depends on the internet and slows down.

quiz.q: An NLTK function raises a LookupError mentioning 'punkt_tab'. What is the fix?
quiz.explain: The sentence-splitting model is a separate data package that must be downloaded.

quiz.q: How do you make NLTK use data from /opt/nltk_data on a server?
options: Copy it into NLTK's own install folder
Set the NLTK_DATA environment variable to that directory
It is impossible; data must be in the home folder
quiz.explain: NLTK_DATA adds that folder to the list of places NLTK searches.

concepts.name: Sentence and word tokenization
concepts.summary: Split text into sentences with sent_tokenize, and into words and punctuation with word_tokenize.
concepts.why: Every later step counts, labels or sorts these pieces, and naive splitting gets punctuation and abbreviations wrong.
concepts.body:
Before a program can count or study words, it has to know where each one starts and ends. Splitting raw text into pieces is called **tokenization**, and each piece (a word, a number or a punctuation mark) is a **token**.

NLTK has two main functions for it:
- `nltk.sent_tokenize(text)` splits text into sentences. It uses **Punkt**, a pretrained model that learned from lots of text that `Dr.` or `U.S.` usually don't end a sentence.
- `nltk.word_tokenize(text)` splits a sentence into word and punctuation tokens.

Why not just `text.split()`? Splitting on spaces leaves punctuation stuck to words (`"world!"`) and can't separate contractions. `word_tokenize` turns `"Don't"` into `["Do", "n't"]` and `"$3.50"` into `["$", "3.50"]`. These odd-looking splits follow the **Penn Treebank**, a big collection of hand-labelled English sentences. NLTK's later tools learned from it and expect the same splits.

Both functions accept `language=` (for example `"german"`) to use another language's Punkt model.

For special cases NLTK has tokenizer objects. You create one by calling its name, like `TweetTokenizer()`, then call its `.tokenize(text)` method:
- `TweetTokenizer` keeps emoticons, hashtags and @handles whole, and can shorten stretched words like "sooooo" (`reduce_len=True`).
- `RegexpTokenizer(r"\w+")` keeps only the text that matches a pattern.
- `wordpunct_tokenize(text)`, a plain function, splits at every punctuation mark.

The pattern in `RegexpTokenizer(r"\w+")` is a **regular expression**: a small language for describing the shape of text. `\w+` means "one or more letters, digits or underscores, one after another", so punctuation is left out. The `r` before the quotes keeps the backslash exactly as typed.

Tokenizers don't change capital letters or remove anything. Lowercasing and dropping common words are separate clean-up steps you choose for the task: a program judging whether a review is positive needs `"NOT"` and `"!"`, which a program finding a text's topic might throw away.
concepts.code:
from nltk.tokenize import (sent_tokenize, word_tokenize,
                           TweetTokenizer, RegexpTokenizer)

text = "Dr. Smith paid $3.50 in the U.S. yesterday. Don't worry, it's fine!"
print(sent_tokenize(text))
# ['Dr. Smith paid $3.50 in the U.S. yesterday.', "Don't worry, it's fine!"]

print(word_tokenize("Don't worry, it's fine!"))
# ['Do', "n't", 'worry', ',', 'it', "'s", 'fine', '!']

print("Don't worry, it's fine!".split())
# ["Don't", 'worry,', "it's", 'fine!']

tweet = "@ana loving #NLP sooooo much :-)"
print(TweetTokenizer(strip_handles=True, reduce_len=True).tokenize(tweet))
# ['loving', '#NLP', 'sooo', 'much', ':-)']

print(RegexpTokenizer(r"\w+").tokenize("Hello, world! 42 times."))
# ['Hello', 'world', '42', 'times']
takeaways: sent_tokenize uses the Punkt model to handle abbreviations like 'Dr.'
word_tokenize splits off punctuation and contractions ('n't', "'s")
TweetTokenizer and RegexpTokenizer handle social media text and custom patterns
Tokenizing doesn't lowercase or filter; that is a separate step
pitfalls: Using str.split() and then counting 'fine!' and 'fine' as different words.

quiz.q: What does `word_tokenize("can't")` return?
quiz.explain: Penn Treebank rules split off the "n't" part, which leaves 'ca'.

quiz.q: Why does sent_tokenize not split after 'Dr.' in 'Dr. Smith arrived.'?
options: The Punkt model learned that 'Dr.' is an abbreviation
quiz.explain: Punkt is trained to recognise abbreviations that don't end sentences.

concepts.name: Frequency counts and stopwords
concepts.summary: Count tokens with FreqDist, remove stopwords, and find the words that best describe a text.
concepts.why: Counting words is the first look at any collection of text and the starting point for finding what it is about.
concepts.body:
`nltk.FreqDist(tokens)` counts how often each token occurs; the name is short for **frequency distribution**. It is a kind of `collections.Counter` with extras, so everything a Counter does still works: `fd["word"]`, `fd.most_common(10)`. The extras: `fd.N()` (total tokens), `fd.B()` (distinct tokens), `fd.freq(w)` (that word's share of all tokens), `fd.hapaxes()` (words seen only once) and `fd.plot(20)`, which draws a chart if the matplotlib library is installed.

Raw counts are dominated by **stopwords**: very common words such as "the", "of" and "and", which say little about the topic. `nltk.corpus.stopwords.words("english")` returns a list of about 200 of them. Put it in a `set`, because checking whether a word is in a set is much faster than searching a list. Lists exist for many other languages.

A typical clean-up before counting:
- lowercase tokens so "The" and "the" merge,
- keep only alphabetic tokens (`w.isalpha()`) to drop punctuation and numbers,
- remove stopwords.

Be deliberate. The stopword list includes "not", "no" and "nor", and removing them turns "not good" into "good" when you judge positive or negative tone. Texts from one subject area also have their own uninformative words ("patient" in hospital notes), which you add to the set.

`ConditionalFreqDist` keeps a separate count for each condition, for example word counts per genre or per author. You give it `(condition, word)` pairs: `ConditionalFreqDist((genre, w) for genre in genres for w in words(genre))`, then ask `cfd["news"].most_common(5)`.
concepts.code:
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import stopwords
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize

text = '''The cat sat on the mat. The dog sat on the log.
The cat and the dog are not friends, but the cat likes the mat.'''

tokens = [w.lower() for w in word_tokenize(text) if w.isalpha()]
fd = nltk.FreqDist(tokens)
print(fd.most_common(3))       # [('the', 8), ('cat', 3), ('sat', 2)]
print(fd.N(), fd.B())          # 26 13

stop = set(stopwords.words("english"))
print(len(stop), "not" in stop)                # 198 True (count varies by version)
content = [w for w in tokens if w not in stop]
print(nltk.FreqDist(content).most_common(3))   # [('cat', 3), ('sat', 2), ('mat', 2)]

cfd = nltk.ConditionalFreqDist((len(w), w) for w in content)
print(sorted(cfd[3]))          # ['cat', 'dog', 'log', 'mat', 'sat']
takeaways: FreqDist is a Counter with extras: most_common, N, B, freq, hapaxes
Lowercase and drop non-alphabetic tokens before counting
Use a set of stopwords; the English list includes 'not' and 'no'
ConditionalFreqDist keeps a separate count per condition
pitfalls: Removing NLTK stopwords before judging positive or negative tone, which deletes 'not' and flips meanings.

quiz.q: Why convert `stopwords.words('english')` to a set before filtering?
options: Checking `w in a_set` is fast, while `w in a_list` checks items one by one
The list contains duplicates that break filtering
quiz.explain: A set finds an item directly through its hash; a list is searched from the start.

concepts.name: Built-in corpora and corpus readers
concepts.summary: Explore Gutenberg, Brown, movie_reviews and other built-in text collections, and load your own files the same way.
concepts.why: Ready-made text collections give you real, often labelled text to practise on, and corpus readers are how NLTK loads any set of documents.
concepts.body:
A **corpus** (plural *corpora*) is a collection of texts gathered for study: a shelf of books, a pile of news articles, a set of reviews. NLTK can download dozens of them through `nltk.corpus`, each fetched like any other data package.

Each corpus comes with a **corpus reader**, an object that offers the same methods for every corpus:
- `fileids()`: the names of the documents in the corpus
- `raw(fileid)`: one document as a single string
- `words(fileid)`: its word tokens; `sents(fileid)`: its sentences, each a list of tokens
- `categories()` and `words(categories="news")` for corpora sorted into groups, such as `brown` and `movie_reviews`
- tagged corpora add `tagged_words()` and `tagged_sents()`, which pair each word with its grammar label (noun, verb...)

Some favourites: `gutenberg` (classic books), `brown` (a mix of 15 genres, every word labelled noun, verb and so on), `movie_reviews` (2,000 reviews, each labelled positive or negative), `reuters`, `inaugural` (US presidents' speeches) and `treebank`.

Reader methods don't load everything at once. They return **corpus views**, which look like lists but read from disk only the parts you actually use. Even a huge corpus doesn't fill your computer's memory until you loop over all of it or turn it into a real list with `list()`.

To use your own documents, point a reader at a folder. `PlaintextCorpusReader(root, r".*\.txt")` reads every file whose name matches the pattern (here, every file ending in `.txt`) and splits it into tokens for you. In recent versions (NLTK 3.10.3 and later), readers only open files inside folders NLTK trusts, so first add your folder to `nltk.data.path` (or `NLTK_DATA`). You then get the same `words()`, `sents()` and `categories()` methods, ready for counting.

`nltk.Text(words)` wraps tokens for exploring: `concordance("word")` shows every place a word occurs along with the words around it, and `similar()` lists words used in similar places.
concepts.code:
import os
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import brown, gutenberg, movie_reviews
from nltk.corpus.reader import PlaintextCorpusReader

print(gutenberg.fileids()[:3])     # ['austen-emma.txt', 'austen-persuasion.txt', 'austen-sense.txt']
print(len(gutenberg.words("austen-emma.txt")))   # 192427

print(brown.categories()[:4])      # ['adventure', 'belles_lettres', 'editorial', 'fiction']
print(brown.tagged_words(categories="news")[:2])  # [('The', 'AT'), ('Fulton', 'NP-TL')]

print(movie_reviews.categories())  # ['neg', 'pos']
print(len(movie_reviews.fileids("pos")))         # 1000

os.makedirs("mydocs", exist_ok=True)               # create the folder
nltk.data.path.append(os.path.abspath("mydocs"))   # needed in NLTK 3.10.3+: let NLTK read it
with open("mydocs/a.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Small corpora are easy. Readers tokenize for you.")
mine = PlaintextCorpusReader("mydocs", r".*\.txt")  # every .txt file
print(mine.fileids(), len(mine.sents("a.txt")))  # ['a.txt'] 2
print(mine.words()[:4])            # ['Small', 'corpora', 'are', 'easy']
takeaways: Corpus readers share fileids, raw, words, sents and categories
Results are corpus views that read from disk only as needed
brown, movie_reviews and treebank come labelled
PlaintextCorpusReader turns your own folder into a corpus
pitfalls: Calling list() on a huge corpus view again and again instead of looping over it once.

quiz.q: What does `movie_reviews.words(categories='pos')` give you?
options: The file names of positive reviews
A single string of positive text
Tokens from all positive reviews, as a list-like corpus view
quiz.explain: words() returns tokens and the categories filter selects positive files.

concepts.name: Stemming with Porter and Snowball
concepts.summary: Cut words down to a shared stem with PorterStemmer, SnowballStemmer and LancasterStemmer, and know where that goes wrong.
concepts.why: Stemming cheaply treats word variants as one word, so a search for 'connect' also finds 'connecting'.
concepts.body:
A search box should treat "connect", "connected", "connecting" and "connection" as the same word. A **stemmer** does this by chopping known endings (and sometimes beginnings) off words with fixed rules, leaving a shared stem: all four become "connect". The stem need not be a real word: "studies" becomes "studi".

NLTK gives you several stemmers. Each is an object you create once and then reuse:
- `PorterStemmer()`: the classic set of rules from 1980, moderate and widely used
- `SnowballStemmer("english")`: an improved version of Porter's rules ("Porter2"), available for many languages (`SnowballStemmer.languages`)
- `LancasterStemmer()`: very aggressive, often cuts too much ("maximum" becomes "maxim")
- `RegexpStemmer` for your own ending rules, written as regular expressions

A stemmer handles one token at a time: `stemmer.stem(word)`. It also lowercases the word.

Stemming goes wrong in two ways. **Over-stemming** merges unrelated words: "universe" and "university" both become "univers". **Under-stemming** misses true relatives, especially irregular forms: "ran" stays "ran" and "better" stays "better".

When to use it: search, and simple programs that sort texts into groups, where speed matters and odd-looking stems are fine. When you need real dictionary words, or correct handling of irregular forms, use lemmatization (a later lesson) instead. Modern AI chat models need neither, because they split words into smaller pieces on their own.
concepts.code:
from nltk.stem import LancasterStemmer, PorterStemmer, SnowballStemmer

words = ["connect", "connected", "connecting", "connection",
         "studies", "running", "ran", "university", "universe", "maximum"]
porter = PorterStemmer()
snow = SnowballStemmer("english")
lanc = LancasterStemmer()

for w in words:
    print(f"{w:11} {porter.stem(w):9} {snow.stem(w):9} {lanc.stem(w)}")
# connection  connect   connect   connect
# studies     studi     studi     study
# ran         ran       ran       ran
# university  univers   univers   univers
# maximum     maximum   maximum   maxim

print("german" in SnowballStemmer.languages)       # True
print(SnowballStemmer("german").stem("Häuser"))    # haus
takeaways: Stemmers strip affixes by rule; stems need not be real words
Snowball (Porter2) is the usual default and supports many languages
Over-stemming merges unrelated words; under-stemming misses irregular forms
Use lemmatization when you need dictionary words
pitfalls: Showing stems such as 'studi' to people, for example as a list of a text's main words.

quiz.q: Which statement about `PorterStemmer().stem('studies')` returning 'studi' is true?
options: It is a bug in NLTK
You must lowercase the input first
Stems are not required to be dictionary words
quiz.explain: Stemming rules only need the variants to end up with the same stem.

quiz.q: 'university' and 'universe' both stem to 'univers'. This is an example of...
quiz.explain: Merging words with different meanings is over-stemming.

concepts.name: Part-of-speech tagging
concepts.summary: Label each token as noun, verb and so on with nltk.pos_tag, read the Penn Treebank tags, and switch to simpler universal tags.
concepts.why: Part-of-speech tags feed lemmatization, phrase finding and many rule-based text patterns.
concepts.body:
At school you learned to label words as nouns, verbs or adjectives. **Part-of-speech tagging** does that automatically: it gives each token a short label called a tag. `nltk.pos_tag(tokens)` takes a tokenized sentence and returns `(word, tag)` pairs.

Behind it is a pretrained model, of a kind called an *averaged perceptron*, that learned from thousands of sentences people tagged by hand (data package `averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng`). Like anything learned from examples, it sometimes guesses wrong.

Tags follow the Penn Treebank **tagset** (its full list of tags), which is detailed:
- nouns: `NN` (singular), `NNS` (plural), `NNP` (a name, like "Paris")
- verbs: `VB` (base form, "go"), `VBD` (past, "went"), `VBG` (-ing form), `VBN` (past participle, "gone"), `VBZ` ("goes")
- `JJ` adjective, `RB` adverb, `DT` determiner ("the", "a"), `IN` preposition ("in", "of"), `PRP` pronoun, `CD` number

`nltk.help.upenn_tagset("VB.*")` explains tags (it needs the `tagsets_json` data). If you only need broad groups, download `universal_tagset` and pass `tagset="universal"` to get `NOUN`, `VERB`, `ADJ`, `ADV`, `DET`, `ADP` (preposition) and so on.

Tag **whole sentences**, not single words or lists of key words. The tagger looks at the neighbouring words, which is how it tells that "permit" is a verb in "refuse to permit us" and a noun in "the permit". It still makes mistakes, especially on words that are usually one part of speech. Removing stopwords or lowercasing before tagging hurts accuracy too.

`pos_tag_sents` tags many sentences in one call. The built-in tagger is fast and reasonable on news-style English. For other languages, chatty text or higher accuracy, people usually move to a newer library such as spaCy. You can also train your own tagger on a tagged corpus.
concepts.code:
import nltk
from nltk import pos_tag, pos_tag_sents, word_tokenize

print(pos_tag(word_tokenize("They refuse to permit us to obtain the refuse permit")))
# [('They', 'PRP'), ('refuse', 'VBP'), ('to', 'TO'), ('permit', 'VB'), ('us', 'PRP'),
#  ('to', 'TO'), ('obtain', 'VB'), ('the', 'DT'), ('refuse', 'NN'), ('permit', 'NN')]
print(pos_tag(word_tokenize("I want to book a flight"))[3])
# ('book', 'NN')  -- taggers make mistakes: here it should be VB

nltk.download("universal_tagset", quiet=True)    # table from detailed to broad tags
print(pos_tag(word_tokenize("Dogs bark loudly"), tagset="universal"))
# [('Dogs', 'NOUN'), ('bark', 'VERB'), ('loudly', 'ADV')]

sents = [word_tokenize(s) for s in ["Time flies.", "She sold 3 cars."]]
for tagged in pos_tag_sents(sents):
    nouns = [w for w, t in tagged if t.startswith("NN")]
    print(nouns)
# ['Time', 'flies']   ('flies' tagged as a plural noun here)
# ['cars']
takeaways: pos_tag returns (word, Penn Treebank tag) pairs
Tags encode detail: NNS plural noun, VBD past-tense verb, JJ adjective
tagset='universal' gives broad groups like NOUN and VERB
Tag full sentences in their original form; neighbouring words drive accuracy
pitfalls: Tagging a list of lowercased key words without their sentence and trusting the tags.

quiz.q: Which tag would the Penn Treebank assign to 'running' in 'She is running'?
quiz.explain: VBG marks the -ing form of a verb.

quiz.q: Why should you POS-tag before removing stopwords?
options: The tagger relies on surrounding words as context
quiz.explain: Neighbouring words like 'to' and 'a' are strong clues for the tag of the next word.

concepts.name: Lemmatization with WordNet
concepts.summary: Map words to dictionary forms with WordNetLemmatizer, and pass the part of speech to get correct results.
concepts.why: Lemmas give clean, readable words for counting and display, and handle irregular forms that stemmers miss.
concepts.body:
A **lemma** is the form of a word you would look up in a dictionary: "ran" becomes "run", "mice" becomes "mouse", "better" becomes "good". Finding it is called **lemmatization**. NLTK does it with **WordNet**, a large English dictionary built for programs (data package `wordnet`): `WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize(word, pos)` looks the word up and applies WordNet's rules for word endings.

The crucial detail is the `pos` argument, the word's part of speech. It defaults to noun (`"n"`), so verbs and adjectives are left alone: `lemmatize("running")` returns "running", while `lemmatize("running", pos="v")` returns "run". Valid values are `"n"`, `"v"`, `"a"` (adjective), `"r"` (adverb) and `"s"` (a special adjective group in WordNet that you rarely need).

In practice you get the part of speech from `pos_tag` and translate its Penn Treebank tags into WordNet's letters: tags starting with `J` are adjectives, `V` verbs, `N` nouns, `R` adverbs.

The lemmatizer expects lowercase input for most words, and returns the word unchanged when WordNet doesn't know it, so names and typos pass through.

Compared with stemming, lemmatization is slower and needs the part of speech, but it produces real words, handles irregular forms and doesn't merge unrelated words. Use it when people will read the output, or when clean words matter, such as finding a text's main topics. spaCy, another NLP library, works out the part of speech for you as one step of its processing.
concepts.code:
from nltk import pos_tag, word_tokenize
from nltk.corpus import wordnet as wn
from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer

lem = WordNetLemmatizer()
print(lem.lemmatize("mice"))               # mouse
print(lem.lemmatize("running"))            # running  (treated as a noun!)
print(lem.lemmatize("running", pos="v"))   # run
print(lem.lemmatize("better", pos="a"))    # good

def to_wn(tag):
    return {"J": wn.ADJ, "V": wn.VERB, "R": wn.ADV}.get(tag[0], wn.NOUN)

sent = "The striped bats were hanging on their feet"
tagged = pos_tag(word_tokenize(sent))
print([lem.lemmatize(w.lower(), to_wn(t)) for w, t in tagged])
# ['the', 'striped', 'bat', 'be', 'hang', 'on', 'their', 'foot']
takeaways: WordNetLemmatizer returns dictionary forms such as run, mouse, good
pos defaults to noun: pass 'v', 'a' or 'r' for verbs, adjectives and adverbs
Map Penn Treebank tags (J, V, N, R) from pos_tag to WordNet's letters
Unknown words are returned unchanged
pitfalls: Calling lemmatize without a POS on verbs and wondering why nothing changes.

quiz.q: What does `WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize('was')` return?
quiz.explain: Without pos='v' the word is treated as a noun, and noun rules strip the final 's' to give 'wa'.

quiz.q: Why does lemmatization usually need a POS tagger in front of it?
options: The correct lemma depends on the part of speech, and the default is noun
quiz.explain: 'saw' is 'see' as a verb but 'saw' as a noun, so the POS decides.

concepts.name: N-grams and collocations
concepts.summary: Build bigrams and other n-grams, and find meaningful phrases with collocation finders and association measures.
concepts.why: Phrases like 'New York' or 'ice cream' mean more than their single words, and n-grams are the basis of the n-gram language models in a later lesson.
concepts.body:
An **n-gram** is a run of n tokens that follow each other: a bigram is two ("New York"), a trigram three. `nltk.ngrams(tokens, n)` produces them as tuples; `nltk.bigrams` and `nltk.trigrams` are shortcuts. Counting them with `FreqDist` shows frequent phrases, but raw counts favour boring pairs such as ("of", "the").

A **collocation** is a pair of words that appear together more often than chance would predict, like "strong tea" (nobody says "powerful tea"). `BigramCollocationFinder.from_words(tokens)` counts all the pairs, and an **association measure**, a formula for how strongly two words belong together, gives each pair a score:
- `BigramAssocMeasures.pmi` (**pointwise mutual information**): high when the two words rarely appear apart, but it overrates rare pairs
- `likelihood_ratio` and `chi_sq`: statistical tests that behave better on typical texts
- `raw_freq`: plain frequency

Filter before scoring. `finder.apply_freq_filter(3)` drops pairs seen fewer than 3 times (essential for PMI). `finder.apply_word_filter(lambda w: w in stop)` drops pairs containing a stopword; `lambda w: w in stop` is a tiny unnamed function that returns True for stopwords. Then `finder.nbest(measure, 10)` returns the top pairs. Trigram versions exist too.

`nltk.Text(tokens).collocation_list()` gives a quick default list.

Uses: spotting phrases before working out a text's topics, building lists of important phrases, and giving text-sorting programs better input. `MWETokenizer` (multi-word expression tokenizer) can then join phrases such as `("New", "York")` into a single token.
concepts.code:
import nltk
from nltk.collocations import BigramAssocMeasures, BigramCollocationFinder
from nltk.corpus import gutenberg, stopwords

tokens = ["machine", "learning", "is", "fun", "and", "machine", "learning", "is", "hard"]
print(list(nltk.bigrams(tokens))[:3])
# [('machine', 'learning'), ('learning', 'is'), ('is', 'fun')]
print(nltk.FreqDist(nltk.ngrams(tokens, 3)).most_common(1))
# [(('machine', 'learning', 'is'), 2)]

words = [w.lower() for w in gutenberg.words("austen-emma.txt") if w.isalpha()]
stop = set(stopwords.words("english"))
finder = BigramCollocationFinder.from_words(words)
finder.apply_freq_filter(5)
finder.apply_word_filter(lambda w: w in stop)
m = BigramAssocMeasures()
print(finder.nbest(m.likelihood_ratio, 4))
# [('mr', 'knightley'), ('mrs', 'weston'), ('frank', 'churchill'), ('mr', 'elton')]

mwe = nltk.MWETokenizer([("machine", "learning")])
print(mwe.tokenize(tokens)[:2])    # ['machine_learning', 'is']
takeaways: nltk.ngrams and nltk.bigrams produce tuples of consecutive tokens
Collocation finders score pairs with PMI, likelihood ratio or chi-square
Apply frequency and stopword filters before ranking
MWETokenizer joins known phrases into single tokens
pitfalls: Ranking by PMI without a frequency filter, so pairs of one-off rare words dominate.

quiz.q: Why does PMI without a frequency filter often rank strange pairs first?
options: Two rare words seen together once get a very high score
quiz.explain: PMI compares how often the words appear together with how often each appears at all; for two rare words seen together once, that ratio is extreme.

concepts.name: Sentiment analysis with VADER
concepts.summary: Score how positive or negative short texts are with VADER's word list and rules, and read its compound score.
concepts.why: VADER gives a solid first sentiment score for reviews and social media in a few lines, with no labelled examples needed.
concepts.body:
**Sentiment analysis** means judging whether a text sounds positive, negative or neutral. **VADER** (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner) is a rule-based tool for it, tuned for social media. It relies on a **lexicon**: a word list in which every word has a score, well above zero for words like "great" and well below for words like "awful".

It needs the `vader_lexicon` data package. Create an analyzer with `SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()` and call its `polarity_scores(text)` method to get a dict:
- `neg`, `neu`, `pos`: how much of the text is negative, neutral and positive (they add up to about 1)
- `compound`: one overall score from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive)

The usual thresholds: compound >= 0.05 is positive, <= -0.05 negative, otherwise neutral.

VADER is more than a word list. Its rules handle:
- **negation**: "not good" flips the score
- **intensifiers**: "very good" scores above "good"; "kind of good" below it
- **capitals and punctuation**: "GOOD!!!" scores higher than "good"
- **"but"**: the part after "but" counts more
- emoticons, common slang and emoji

Feed it raw text, not stemmed or lowercased tokens, because capitals, punctuation and words like "not" carry the signal.

Limits: it doesn't understand sarcasm, words whose meaning depends on the subject ("unpredictable" is good for a thriller, bad for a car) or long documents. For a longer text, score each sentence and combine the results, for example by averaging. Before trusting it, compare its answers with texts from your own subject area that people have labelled. When you have many labelled examples, a trained classifier (an Advanced lesson) usually does better.
concepts.code:
from nltk.sentiment import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer

sia = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()

def label(text):
    c = sia.polarity_scores(text)["compound"]
    return "pos" if c >= 0.05 else "neg" if c <= -0.05 else "neu"

print(sia.polarity_scores("The food was good."))
# {'neg': 0.0, 'neu': 0.508, 'pos': 0.492, 'compound': 0.4404}

for t in ["The food was good.", "The food was not good.",
          "The food was VERY GOOD!!!", "The food was good, but the service was awful.",
          "The table is made of wood."]:
    print(f"{sia.polarity_scores(t)['compound']:+.3f} {label(t)}  {t}")
# +0.440 pos  The food was good.
# -0.341 neg  The food was not good.
# +0.760 pos  The food was VERY GOOD!!!
# -0.468 neg  The food was good, but the service was awful.
# +0.000 neu  The table is made of wood.
takeaways: polarity_scores returns neg/neu/pos shares and a compound score
compound >= 0.05 positive, <= -0.05 negative is the usual rule
Rules handle negation, intensifiers, capitals, punctuation and 'but'
Give it raw text and check it on labelled examples from your own subject area
pitfalls: Lowercasing and stripping punctuation before VADER, which throws away intensity cues.

quiz.q: Which input will get the highest compound score from VADER?
options: The movie was kind of good
quiz.explain: Capitalisation and exclamation marks are treated as intensifiers.

concepts.name: Text classification with Naive Bayes
concepts.summary: Turn documents into feature dicts, train NLTK's NaiveBayesClassifier, measure accuracy and see which features matter most.
concepts.why: Building a classifier end to end shows the core workflow of learning from labelled examples: features, training, and testing on separate data.
concepts.body:
A **classifier** is a program that sorts things into categories, such as positive or negative reviews. Instead of writing its rules yourself, you **train** it: you show it many examples whose correct label you already know, and it learns which clues go with which label. Learning from labelled examples like this is called supervised learning.

NLTK classifiers don't read text directly. Each example becomes a **featureset**: a `dict` of clues (features) about the document, paired with its label. You write a **feature extractor**, a function that builds that dict, for example `{"has(great)": True, "has(awful)": False, ...}` over a chosen list of words.

The workflow:
- build `(features, label)` pairs for every document,
- shuffle them and split them into a **training set** to learn from and a **test set** kept aside to check the result (never test on the examples it learned from),
- `clf = nltk.NaiveBayesClassifier.train(train_set)`,
- `nltk.classify.accuracy(clf, test_set)`: the share of test examples it gets right,
- `clf.classify(features)` for one prediction, `clf.prob_classify(...)` for probabilities,
- `clf.show_most_informative_features(10)` to see which features drive its decisions.

**Naive Bayes** combines, for each label, how likely each feature is under that label. It's "naive" because it assumes the features don't affect one another. That's false for language, but it trains instantly, copes well with thousands of mostly-False features and makes a strong first model for sentiment and topic tasks.

Choosing the word list is a design decision; the 2,000 most frequent words is a common start. With a True/False feature for every listed word, inputs should look like the training documents: a five-word snippet is almost all False and gets classified poorly. Build the word list from the training set only. Choosing it with the test set lets knowledge of the test leak in, and accuracy looks better than it really is.

`nltk.classify.SklearnClassifier` wraps a model from scikit-learn, the main Python machine learning library (for example `LogisticRegression`), so it accepts the same featuresets; it usually beats Naive Bayes. For bigger projects, scikit-learn's own text tools or modern neural network models are the usual next step.
concepts.code:
import random
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import movie_reviews as mr

docs = [(list(mr.words(f)), cat) for cat in mr.categories() for f in mr.fileids(cat)]
random.seed(0)
random.shuffle(docs)
train_docs, test_docs = docs[:1600], docs[1600:]

fd = nltk.FreqDist(w.lower() for words, _ in train_docs for w in words if w.isalpha())
vocab = [w for w, _ in fd.most_common(2000)]          # from training data only

def features(words):
    present = set(w.lower() for w in words)
    return {f"has({w})": (w in present) for w in vocab}

train_set = [(features(d), c) for d, c in train_docs]
test_set = [(features(d), c) for d, c in test_docs]
clf = nltk.NaiveBayesClassifier.train(train_set)
print(round(nltk.classify.accuracy(clf, test_set), 2))   # about 0.8
print(clf.classify(test_set[0][0]), test_set[0][1])  # predicted vs gold label
clf.show_most_informative_features(3)
# has(outstanding) = True   pos : neg = 22.2 : 1.0 ...
takeaways: Features are dicts produced by your own extractor function
Train on the training set, measure accuracy on a separate test set
NaiveBayesClassifier is fast and easy to inspect with most_informative_features
SklearnClassifier plugs scikit-learn models into the same workflow
pitfalls: Building the word list from all documents, including the test set, which makes accuracy look better than it is.

quiz.q: What is the input format NLTK's NaiveBayesClassifier.train expects?
options: Two separate lists: texts and labels
quiz.explain: Each training example is a featureset dict paired with its label.

quiz.q: Why is Naive Bayes called 'naive'?
options: It assumes features are independent of each other, given the label
quiz.explain: It multiplies per-feature probabilities as if features didn't influence each other.

concepts.name: Chunking and named entities
concepts.summary: Group tagged words into phrases with RegexpParser rules, and find names of people, places and companies with ne_chunk.
concepts.why: Phrases such as 'the old cat' and names such as 'Seattle' are what most programs that pull facts out of text are after.
concepts.body:
**Chunking** groups part-of-speech-tagged tokens into short phrases that don't overlap, such as noun phrases ("the little yellow dog"). It doesn't work out the full grammar of the sentence, which is why it's also called shallow parsing. `nltk.RegexpParser(grammar)` takes rules written as regular expressions over **tags**, not words:

```text
NP: {<DT>?<JJ>*<NN.*>+}
```

This says a noun phrase (`NP`) is an optional determiner, any number of adjectives, then one or more nouns. `<NN.*>` matches NN, NNS, NNP and NNPS. Rules can also **chink**, cutting tokens back out of a chunk, with `}...{`, and you can define several labels, applied in order.

`parser.parse(tagged)` returns an `nltk.Tree`, a **parse tree**: a nested structure where the top node `S` (sentence) contains a smaller tree for each chunk, and plain `(word, tag)` tuples for everything else. Pick out chunks with `tree.subtrees(filter=lambda t: t.label() == "NP")` and get their words with `t.leaves()`.

**Named entity recognition** (NER) finds names in text and says what kind they are. `nltk.ne_chunk(tagged)` does it with a pretrained model (data `maxent_ne_chunker_tab` plus `words`) and labels `PERSON`, `ORGANIZATION`, `GPE` (geo-political entity: a country, state or city), `LOCATION` and others. `binary=True` simply marks them all `NE`.

`nltk.chunk.tree2conlltags(tree)` turns the tree into **IOB tags**, one per token: `B-NP` begins a chunk, `I-NP` is inside one, `O` is outside any chunk. This is the standard format for training and checking chunkers.

NLTK's NER is old and clearly less accurate than spaCy or modern neural network models; the example shows it splitting a person's name and mislabelling a company. Use it to learn the ideas or for quick experiments. RegexpParser stays handy for precise, rule-based phrase patterns.
concepts.code:
import nltk
from nltk import ne_chunk, pos_tag, word_tokenize

tagged = pos_tag(word_tokenize("The little yellow dog barked at the old cat"))
parser = nltk.RegexpParser("NP: {<DT>?<JJ>*<NN.*>+}")
tree = parser.parse(tagged)
for np_ in tree.subtrees(filter=lambda t: t.label() == "NP"):
    print(" ".join(w for w, t in np_.leaves()))
# The little yellow dog
# the old cat

print(nltk.chunk.tree2conlltags(tree)[:3])
# [('The', 'DT', 'B-NP'), ('little', 'JJ', 'I-NP'), ('yellow', 'JJ', 'I-NP')]

sent = "Barack Obama visited Microsoft in Seattle last week."
ents = ne_chunk(pos_tag(word_tokenize(sent)))
for t in ents.subtrees(filter=lambda t: t.label() != "S"):
    print(t.label(), " ".join(w for w, _ in t.leaves()))
# PERSON Barack
# PERSON Obama
# PERSON Microsoft     <- wrong label, and the name above was split in two
# GPE Seattle          (output from NLTK 3.10's model)
takeaways: RegexpParser rules are regular expressions over part-of-speech tags
Chunk results are nltk.Tree objects; filter subtrees by label
ne_chunk labels PERSON, ORGANIZATION, GPE and more
IOB tags (B-, I-, O) write chunks as one tag per token
pitfalls: Writing chunk patterns over words instead of tags, e.g. <dog> rather than <NN>.

quiz.q: Which tokens does the rule `NP: {<DT>?<JJ>*<NN>}` chunk in 'a big red ball' tagged DT JJ JJ NN?
quiz.explain: The optional determiner, any number of adjectives and the noun all match.

quiz.q: In NLTK's NER output, what does the label GPE stand for?
options: Geo-Political Entity, such as a country or city
quiz.explain: GPE covers places with governments: countries, states, cities.

concepts.name: WordNet: synsets and word relations
concepts.summary: Navigate WordNet synsets, definitions, synonyms, hypernyms and similarity scores.
concepts.why: WordNet adds knowledge of meanings, synonyms and 'is a kind of' links to rule-based programs, for example to widen a search with related words.
concepts.body:
**WordNet** is a big English dictionary built for programs. Instead of listing words alphabetically, it groups them into **synsets**: sets of synonyms that share one meaning. Access it with `from nltk.corpus import wordnet as wn` (data package `wordnet`).

- `wn.synsets("bank")` lists every meaning of a word, with names like `bank.n.01` (word, part of speech, sense number). Filter with `pos=wn.VERB`.
- `syn.definition()` and `syn.examples()` explain a meaning.
- `syn.lemmas()` gives the words in the synset; `lemma.name()` the text, and `lemma.antonyms()` opposites.

Synsets are linked to each other:
- **hypernyms** are more general (a dog is a kind of canine) and **hyponyms** more specific (a puppy is a kind of dog)
- **meronyms** and holonyms link parts and wholes (a tree has a trunk)
- `syn.hypernym_paths()` gives the chains of ever more general meanings up to the top, `entity.n.01`, and `lowest_common_hypernyms(other)` the closest meaning two synsets share

Similarity measures compare two meanings by their place in this hierarchy: `path_similarity` (0 to 1, from the shortest path between them), `wup_similarity` (Wu-Palmer, based on how deep their closest shared ancestor sits), and measures such as `res_similarity` that also need word counts from a corpus.

The hard part is the **word sense**: a word has several synsets, and picking the right one needs the surrounding words. `nltk.wsd.lesk(context_tokens, word)` is a simple first attempt: it picks the sense whose definition shares the most words with the sentence. With the Open Multilingual WordNet data (`omw-1.4`, or `omw-2.0` in the newest releases), `lemma_names(lang="fra")` gives the words in other languages.
concepts.code:
from nltk.corpus import wordnet as wn

senses = wn.synsets("bank")
print(len(senses) > 10, senses[0].name())     # True bank.n.01
print(wn.synset("bank.n.02").definition())
# a financial institution that accepts deposits and channels the money ...

dog = wn.synset("dog.n.01")
print(dog.hypernyms())         # [Synset('domestic_animal.n.01'), Synset('canine.n.02')]
print([l.name() for l in wn.synset("good.a.01").lemmas()[0].antonyms()])   # ['bad']

cat, car = wn.synset("cat.n.01"), wn.synset("car.n.01")
print(round(dog.path_similarity(cat), 2), round(dog.path_similarity(car), 2))
# 0.2 0.08  (dog is closer to cat than to car)
print(round(dog.wup_similarity(cat), 2))      # 0.86
print(dog.lowest_common_hypernyms(cat))       # [Synset('carnivore.n.01')]
print(dog.lemma_names("fra"))  # ['canis_familiaris', 'chien'] (needs omw data)
takeaways: Synsets are meanings; a word usually has several
definition(), examples(), lemmas() describe a synset
Hypernyms/hyponyms form an is-a hierarchy you can walk
path_similarity and wup_similarity compare senses, not words
pitfalls: Taking `wn.synsets(word)[0]` as the meaning without considering context.

quiz.q: What is a hypernym of 'dog.n.01'?
quiz.explain: A hypernym is a more general concept; canine is a broader category containing dogs.

quiz.q: Why do similarity functions take synsets rather than words?
options: Words are too long to compare
A word can have many senses, and similarity is defined between specific meanings
quiz.explain: 'bank' as a river edge and as a lender would have very different similarities to 'money'.

concepts.name: Context-free grammars and parsing
concepts.summary: Write a context-free grammar, parse sentences into trees with chart parsers, and see why ambiguity makes parsing hard.
concepts.why: Parsing shows how a sentence's structure can be written down, and why ambiguity is the central problem of NLP.
concepts.body:
A **context-free grammar** (CFG) describes how sentences are built using rewrite rules. Each rule says a label can be replaced by a sequence of labels or words. `nltk.CFG.fromstring` reads rules like these:

```text
S -> NP VP
NP -> Det N | Det N PP | 'I'
VP -> V NP | VP PP
PP -> P NP
```

`S -> NP VP` reads "a sentence is a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase", and `|` separates alternatives. Labels such as S, NP and VP are **non-terminals**: they get rewritten again and again until only actual words (in quotes) remain. A parser finds every tree that turns the start label `S` into exactly your list of tokens.

`nltk.ChartParser(grammar)` is a **chart parser**: it saves every partial result in a table (the chart) and reuses it, instead of re-trying the same sub-phrases over and over. That trick is called dynamic programming. `RecursiveDescentParser` and `ShiftReduceParser` exist for teaching but are slower or miss parses. The recursive descent parser also loops forever on rules whose right side starts with their own label, like `VP -> VP PP`.

`parser.parse(tokens)` yields `nltk.Tree` objects. Trees support `tree.label()`, `tree.leaves()`, indexing into their children, `tree.pretty_print()` to draw the tree with text characters, and `tree.productions()` to list the rules used.

The classic lesson is **ambiguity**: "I shot an elephant in my pajamas" has two parses, depending on whether "in my pajamas" belongs to the shooting (the verb phrase) or to the elephant (the noun phrase). Real grammars give long sentences hundreds or thousands of parses. A probabilistic CFG (`nltk.PCFG`, parsed with `ViterbiParser`) gives each rule a probability and ranks the trees. Modern parsers such as spaCy's learn sentence structure from large hand-parsed corpora instead of hand-written rules.

Hand-written CFGs are still useful for small, fixed languages, such as the commands a text adventure game or a simple voice assistant accepts.
concepts.code:
import nltk

grammar = nltk.CFG.fromstring('''
S -> NP VP
PP -> P NP
NP -> Det N | Det N PP | 'I'
VP -> V NP | VP PP
Det -> 'an' | 'my'
N -> 'elephant' | 'pajamas'
V -> 'shot'
P -> 'in'
''')
parser = nltk.ChartParser(grammar)
tokens = "I shot an elephant in my pajamas".split()
trees = list(parser.parse(tokens))
print(len(trees))                    # 2  -- structurally ambiguous
for t in trees:
    print(t)
# (S (NP I) (VP (VP (V shot) (NP (Det an) (N elephant))) (PP (P in) ...)))
# (S (NP I) (VP (V shot) (NP (Det an) (N elephant) (PP (P in) ...))))
print(trees[0].label(), trees[0].leaves()[:2])   # S ['I', 'shot']
takeaways: CFG rules rewrite labels until only words remain
ChartParser finds all parses efficiently by reusing partial results
Parse results are nltk.Tree objects with label(), leaves(), pretty_print()
Ambiguity yields many trees; probabilistic grammars and learned parsers rank them
pitfalls: Using RecursiveDescentParser with a rule like VP -> VP PP, which never finishes.

quiz.q: Why does 'I shot an elephant in my pajamas' get two parse trees?
options: 'in my pajamas' can attach either to the verb phrase or to the noun phrase
'shot' is both a noun and a verb
quiz.explain: Who is wearing the pajamas depends on whether 'in my pajamas' attaches to the verb phrase or the noun phrase.

concepts.name: N-gram language models with nltk.lm
concepts.summary: Train MLE, Laplace and Kneser-Ney n-gram models, handle padding and unknown words, generate text and compute perplexity.
concepts.why: N-gram language models are the ancestors of today's LLMs and still teach the core ideas: counting, unseen words and measuring quality.
concepts.body:
A **language model** gives a probability to a sequence of words: how likely it is that someone would write it. An n-gram model simplifies this. It predicts each word from only the previous n-1 words, `P(word | previous words)`, estimated from counts in training text. A bigram model looks at just one previous word.

`nltk.lm` organises this:
- `padded_everygram_pipeline(n, sentences)` adds start and end markers `<s>` and `</s>` to each sentence (padding), and produces all 1- to n-grams for training plus the list of every word seen.
- Model types: `MLE` (maximum likelihood estimate: plain relative frequencies), `Laplace` (add one to every count), `Lidstone(gamma)`, `KneserNeyInterpolated` and `WittenBellInterpolated`.
- `lm.fit(train, vocab)`, then `lm.score(word, context)`, `lm.logscore` (log base 2), `lm.generate(n, text_seed=..., random_seed=...)`.

The core problem is sparsity: most possible n-grams never appear in the training text. MLE gives every unseen n-gram probability 0, so one new bigram makes a whole test sentence "impossible". **Smoothing** fixes this by taking a little probability from seen n-grams and sharing it among unseen ones. Laplace does it crudely; Kneser-Ney, which also considers in how many different contexts a word appears, is the classic best performer.

The `Vocabulary` replaces rare or unseen words with `<UNK>` (unknown), controlled by `unk_cutoff`, so words the model never saw don't break scoring.

**Perplexity**, `lm.perplexity(test_ngrams)`, measures how surprised the model is by test text: 2 to the power of the average negative log2 probability per word. Lower is better, and it roughly means "how many words the model is choosing between" at each step. A single probability of 0 makes it infinite. Compare perplexities only between models with the same vocabulary.
concepts.code:
from nltk.lm import MLE, KneserNeyInterpolated, Laplace
from nltk.lm.preprocessing import padded_everygram_pipeline
from nltk.util import bigrams, pad_sequence

corpus = [s.split() for s in ["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log",
                              "the cat saw the dog", "a dog sat on a mat"]]
models = {}
for name, cls in [("mle", MLE), ("laplace", Laplace), ("kn", KneserNeyInterpolated)]:
    train, vocab = padded_everygram_pipeline(2, corpus)
    models[name] = cls(2)
    models[name].fit(train, vocab)

mle = models["mle"]
print(mle.counts[["the"]]["cat"], round(mle.score("cat", ["the"]), 3))   # 2 0.333
print(mle.score("log", ["a"]))                                          # 0.0 unseen

test = list(bigrams(pad_sequence("a cat sat on the log".split(), 2,
                                 pad_left=True, left_pad_symbol="<s>",
                                 pad_right=True, right_pad_symbol="</s>")))
for name, m in models.items():
    print(name, round(m.perplexity(test), 2))
# mle inf   (one unseen bigram ruins it)
# laplace 7.04
# kn 4.09
print(mle.generate(5, text_seed=["the"], random_seed=3))   # e.g. ['cat', 'saw', 'the', 'dog', 'sat']
takeaways: N-gram LMs estimate P(word | previous n-1 words) from counts
padded_everygram_pipeline pads sentences and builds training n-grams
MLE gives zero to unseen n-grams; Laplace and Kneser-Ney smooth
Perplexity (lower is better) compares models on the same vocabulary
pitfalls: Comparing perplexities of models trained with different vocabularies or UNK handling.

quiz.q: An MLE bigram model reports infinite perplexity on a test sentence. Why?
options: The test sentence is too long
At least one bigram in it never occurred in training, so its probability is 0
quiz.explain: log(0) is minus infinity, so a single unseen n-gram makes perplexity infinite without smoothing.

concepts.name: Training Punkt and building custom tokenizers
concepts.summary: Adapt sentence splitting to your subject area by training Punkt or adding abbreviations, and build precise word tokenizers with regular expressions.
concepts.why: Pretrained tokenizers break on legal, medical or technical text full of unusual abbreviations, quietly spoiling every later step.
concepts.body:
**Punkt** learns from raw text that nobody has labelled. It works out which words ending in a period are abbreviations, which words often start sentences, and which word pairs often sit together around a period. The models NLTK ships were trained on news text, so abbreviations from other subject areas, such as `approx.`, `Fig.` or `cf.`, can cause false sentence breaks.

Two ways to adapt it:
- **Train** it on a large sample of your own text: `PunktTrainer().train(text, finalize=False)`, then `finalize_training()`, then `PunktSentenceTokenizer(trainer.get_params())`. More text gives better statistics; a few hundred kilobytes is a reasonable start.
- **Patch** its settings directly: add lowercase abbreviations, without the period, to `tokenizer._params.abbrev_types`. Quick and predictable, but the leading underscore marks `_params` as NLTK's internal data, which could change between versions.

`span_tokenize(text)` returns character positions `(start, end)` instead of strings. You need these to map results back to the original document, for example to highlight sentences.

For words, `RegexpTokenizer(pattern)` gives full control. With `gaps=True` the pattern describes the separators instead of the tokens. Start a long pattern with `(?x)` (verbose mode) so you can spread it out with spaces, then handle tricky cases one alternative at a time: abbreviations like `U.S.A.`, hyphenated words, prices and percentages. `MWETokenizer` then joins multi-word phrases, and `TreebankWordDetokenizer` turns tokens back into readable text.

Test tokenizers on real examples from your texts and compare the output before and after each change. Small changes ripple through every count and model built on top.
concepts.code:
from nltk.tokenize import RegexpTokenizer, sent_tokenize
from nltk.tokenize.punkt import PunktSentenceTokenizer, PunktTrainer

text = "Results are shown in Fig. 3 of the paper. Values were approx. 5 mm."
print(sent_tokenize(text))
# ['Results are shown in Fig.', '3 of the paper.', 'Values were approx.', '5 mm.']

trainer = PunktTrainer()
trainer.INCLUDE_ALL_COLLOCS = True
trainer.train("See Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 here. It was approx. 3 cm long. " * 50, finalize=False)
trainer.finalize_training()
tok = PunktSentenceTokenizer(trainer.get_params())
tok._params.abbrev_types.update({"fig", "approx"})   # make sure
print(tok.tokenize(text))
# ['Results are shown in Fig. 3 of the paper.', 'Values were approx. 5 mm.']
print(list(tok.span_tokenize(text)))    # [(0, 41), (42, 67)]

pattern = r'''(?x) (?:[A-Z]\.)+ | \$?\d+(?:\.\d+)?%? | \w+(?:-\w+)* | [^\w\s]'''
print(RegexpTokenizer(pattern).tokenize("The U.S.A. grew 3.5% in well-known $12 deals."))
# ['The', 'U.S.A.', 'grew', '3.5%', 'in', 'well-known', '$12', 'deals', '.']
takeaways: Punkt learns abbreviations and sentence starters from raw text
Train with PunktTrainer on your own texts, or add abbreviations to its settings
span_tokenize returns character positions for mapping back
Verbose (?x) patterns in RegexpTokenizer give precise word rules
pitfalls: Assuming the default sentence splitter works on technical or legal text without checking a sample.

quiz.q: Scientific text is split after 'Fig.' and 'approx.'. What is the most direct fix?
options: Train Punkt on texts from that subject area or add those abbreviations to the tokenizer's settings
quiz.explain: Punkt decides sentence ends from its abbreviation list, which you can learn or extend.

concepts.name: Evaluation: metrics, agreement and BLEU
concepts.summary: Measure NLP systems with precision, recall, F1, confusion matrices, edit distance, annotator agreement and BLEU.
concepts.why: Choosing and computing the right score is what separates a convincing NLP result from a misleading one.
concepts.body:
Accuracy alone hides a lot. If 95% of emails are not spam, a program that never says "spam" is 95% accurate and useless. NLTK has the tools to measure systems properly.

**Precision** asks: of the items the system gave a label, how many really have it? **Recall** asks: of the items that really have the label, how many did the system find? The **F1 score** combines both into one number (their harmonic mean, which stays low if either one is low).

In `nltk.metrics.scores`, `precision(reference, test)`, `recall` and `f_measure` work on **sets** of item ids: one set of the ids that truly have a label (the gold answers) and one set the system gave that label. Compute them per label. `nltk.ConfusionMatrix(gold, predicted)` builds a **confusion matrix**, a grid counting each true label against each predicted one, so you see which labels get mixed up; `.evaluate()` prints a per-label report.

**String distance**: `nltk.edit_distance(a, b)` is the **edit distance** (Levenshtein distance), the fewest single-letter insertions, deletions or replacements that turn one string into the other. `transpositions=True` also counts swapping two neighbouring letters as one step. `jaccard_distance(set_a, set_b)` compares sets. Both help with spelling correction and fuzzy matching.

**Annotator agreement**: before trusting labels, check whether the people who wrote them agree. `nltk.metrics.agreement.AnnotationTask(data)` takes `(coder, item, label)` triples and computes `kappa()`, `pi()` and `alpha()`. **Cohen's kappa** removes the agreement that would happen by chance: 0.8 and above is strong, and below about 0.6 the labelling guidelines need work. A model can't be more reliable than its labels.

**Translation and text generation**: `nltk.translate.bleu_score.sentence_bleu(references, hypothesis)` computes **BLEU**, which scores how many 1- to 4-word sequences of the output also appear in reference translations, with a penalty for output that is too short. `corpus_bleu` combines a whole test set properly (it is not the average of sentence scores). BLEU multiplies the scores for each sequence length, so a short sentence with no matching 4-word sequence scores 0; pass `SmoothingFunction().method1` when scoring single sentences. `meteor_score` and `nist_score` exist too.

Report every score with its exact settings, and always compute it on a test set the system never trained on.
concepts.code:
import nltk
from nltk.metrics import precision, recall, f_measure
from nltk.metrics.agreement import AnnotationTask
from nltk.translate.bleu_score import SmoothingFunction, sentence_bleu

gold = ["pos", "pos", "neg", "neg", "pos", "neg"]
pred = ["pos", "neg", "neg", "neg", "pos", "pos"]
ref = {i for i, g in enumerate(gold) if g == "pos"}
hyp = {i for i, p in enumerate(pred) if p == "pos"}
print(round(precision(ref, hyp), 2), round(recall(ref, hyp), 2), round(f_measure(ref, hyp), 2))
# 0.67 0.67 0.67
print(nltk.ConfusionMatrix(gold, pred)["pos", "neg"])     # 1  gold pos predicted neg

print(nltk.edit_distance("kitten", "sitting"))           # 3

data = [("a1", i, g) for i, g in enumerate(gold)] + [("a2", i, p) for i, p in enumerate(pred)]
print(round(AnnotationTask(data=data).kappa(), 2))        # 0.33  weak agreement

reference = ["the cat is on the mat".split()]
smooth = SmoothingFunction().method1
print(round(sentence_bleu(reference, "the cat is on the mat".split()), 2))   # 1.0
print(round(sentence_bleu(reference, "the cat sat on mat".split(), smoothing_function=smooth), 2))
# 0.11  low but non-zero thanks to smoothing
takeaways: precision, recall and f_measure take sets of item ids per label
ConfusionMatrix shows which labels get mixed up
Kappa and alpha check that human labels are reliable
Use corpus_bleu for test sets; smooth sentence-level BLEU
pitfalls: Averaging sentence_bleu scores over a test set instead of computing corpus_bleu.

quiz.q: Two annotators agree on 85% of items, but one label covers 80% of the data. Why report Cohen's kappa?
options: Kappa is always higher than raw agreement
Kappa corrects for agreement expected by chance, which is high with a dominant label
Raw agreement can't be computed with two annotators
quiz.explain: With a skewed label distribution, much of the raw agreement would occur by chance.

quiz.q: Why can sentence_bleu return 0 for a reasonable short translation?
options: With no matching 4-grams the combined score becomes 0 unless smoothing is used
quiz.explain: BLEU multiplies the scores for each n-gram length, so a zero for 4-grams makes the whole product 0.
